citation.title: Estimating Causal Effects in Experiments with Network Spillovers

standing_assumptions:
[Nature of the work] The chapter (chapter 16 of the Handbook of Computational Social Science; printed pp. 209–222, PDF pp. 1–14, printed page = PDF page + 208) is an exposition with worked R examples. It has no numbered theorem, proposition, lemma, assumption or proof and no displayed estimator; its two mathematical displays are the exposure mapping (p. 211) and the estimand (p. 212). Note 2 (p. 221, PDF p. 13): “For a formal discussion of the estimators, see Aronow and Samii (2017).” Everything quoted below was read from the page images.
(S1) Population and network. p. 210 (PDF p. 2): “We imagine a situation where an analyst is planning an experiment on a finite population, $U$, of units indexed by $i = 1,...,N$. The units are connected to each other through a network that we represent as an $N \times N$ adjacency matrix, $\theta$, with entries that equal, for example, 0 or 1 (and with 0’s on the diagonal). A value of 1 in row $i$ and column $j$ in the adjacency matrix means that $i$’s potential outcomes might depend on whether or not $j$ is treated (e.g., they may be immediate peers or close to each other in the network). A value of 0 in row $i$ and column $j$ means that $i$’s potential outcomes most certainly do not depend on $j$’s treatment status (e.g., there are no channels through which $j$ could influence $i$, even indirectly). The undirected network in Figure 16.1 would be represented by a symmetric adjacency matrix, with 1’s representing edges between units and 0’s representing the absence of edges.”
(S2) Treatment and design. pp. 210–211 (PDF pp. 2–3): “The experiment is one in which units could be assigned to either a “treatment” or “control” condition. We use an indicator, $z_i \in \{0,1\}$, to denote whether unit $i$ is assigned to treatment ($z_i = 1$) or control $z_i = 0$). The $N \times 1$ vector of treatments for all units is given by $\mathbf{z} = (z_1,...,z_N)'$. Given that treatments are binary, there are, in principle, $2^N$ different treatment assignment profiles that could be constructed. An experimental design assigns some probability, $p_{\mathbf{z}}$, to a treatment profile, $\mathbf{z}$. Under the Bernoulli assignment experimental design, treatments are assigned through independent Bernoulli draws (e.g., independent coin flips), in which case $p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0$ for any of the $2^N$ possible profiles, although $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ would be vanishingly small for some profiles (such as the profile in which $\mathbf{z}$ is a vector of only 0’s). The complete random assignment design, in which $N_1$ units are randomly assigned (without replacement) to treatment and $N_0 = N - N_1$ units to control, yields $p_{\mathbf{z}} = 0$ for any assignment in which more or fewer than $N_1$ units are assigned to treatment, and $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ would otherwise be uniform for all assignments with $N_1$ units assigned to treatment. Other types of experimental designs include various forms of stratified and clustered designs. Let the random $N \times 1$ vector $\mathbf{Z}$ refer to the treatment assignment profile that is ultimately realized, with $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$.”
(S3) Potential outcomes. p. 211 (PDF p. 3): “We define causal effects in terms of how units’ potential outcomes would change as $\mathbf{z}$ changes (Imbens & Rubin, 2015, ch. 1–2). We denote $i$’s potential outcome under treatment assignment vector $\mathbf{z}$ as $y_i(\mathbf{z})$, where $y_i(\cdot)$ is a real-valued function that maps treatment profiles to an individual’s outcome. For unit $i$, the effect of applying treatment profile $\mathbf{z}$ as compared to $\mathbf{z}'$ would be measured in the way that $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ differs from $y_i(\mathbf{z}')$. We focus on effects defined as differences, such as $y_i(\mathbf{z}) - y_i(\mathbf{z}')$.”
(S4) Exposure mapping. p. 211 (PDF p. 3): “Following the approach of Aronow and Samii (2017), we define an exposure mapping, $f(\cdot)$, to establish what we think is the plausible extent and nature of spillover. For a unit $i$, the exposure mapping takes a treatment profile, $\mathbf{z}$, from the experimental design and the interference network, $\theta$, as inputs, and then as an output, it generates an exposure, $d$. The exposure mapping is a way of modeling how different patterns of treatment assignment among peers might induce different potential outcomes. Thus, the exposure mapping translates potential outcomes defined in terms of treatment profiles, $\mathbf{z}$, into potential outcomes defined in terms of exposures, $d$. For example, we might suppose that a given unit’s potential outcomes depend on whether (a) they are treated or (b) any one of their network peers is treated. This would imply an exposure mapping that takes as inputs the assignment profile $\mathbf{z}$ and unit $i$’s row in the adjacency matrix, $\theta_i$, as follows: $$f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = \begin{cases} d_{11}\ (\text{Direct + Indirect Exposure}): & z_i\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0) = 1, \\ d_{10}\ (\text{Isolated Direct Exposure}): & z_i\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0) = 1, \\ d_{01}\ (\text{Indirect Exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0) = 1, \\ d_{00}\ (\text{No Exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0) = 1 \end{cases}$$ This particular exposure mapping implies that each unit $i$ has four potential outcomes, $(y_i(d_{11}), y_i(d_{10}), y_i(d_{01}), y_i(d_{00}))$, which are based on combinations of their own treatment status and whether any of their peers is treated.” (The last clause is on p. 212, PDF p. 4. The display prints the four labels without spaces between words. The product $\mathbf{z}'\theta_i$ is as printed; see P044-T9.)
(S5) Estimand. p. 212 (PDF p. 4): “These exposure-based potential outcomes define causal effects. Under the exposure mapping defined above, the effect for unit $i$ of being treated along with their peers, as compared to being in a situation where neither the unit nor any of their peers are treated, is given by $y_i(d_{11}) - y_i(d_{00})$ . Insofar as this effect differs from the effect of isolated direct exposure ($y_i(d_{10}) - y_i(d_{00})$), then network spillover effects are meaningful in altering outcomes for those who are directly treated. Once the treatment profile, $\mathbf{Z}$, is drawn, units will be assigned to the corresponding exposure, $d$, and will reveal the associated potential outcome, $y_i(d)$. For a given unit, other exposures are counterfactual and not directly observable. For this reason, we do not focus on trying to estimate unit-level effects, but rather on average effects for the entire population, $$\tau(d,d') = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_i(d) - y_i(d')),$$ where $d$ and $d'$ are two different possible exposures.”
(S6) The recipe for exposure probabilities. p. 212 (PDF p. 4): “Moreover, with the network adjacency matrix and exposure mapping in hand, these probabilities of exposure can be computed directly from the experimental design. Specifically, one can simulate treatment assignments based on the experimental design, feed them through the exposure mapping for each unit, and then determine each unit’s probabilities of falling into any of the exposure conditions.” p. 214 (PDF p. 6): “To compute the exposure probabilities, we first need to simulate the set of all possible (or a large random sample of all possible) treatment assignments according to the experimental design. In this case, a proportion $p = 0.1$ of the $N = 1000$ units in the network is randomly assigned to treatment with uniform probability on the basis of complete random assignment. Because the set of all possible treatment assignments is very large $\binom{N}{pN}$, we compute a set of $R$ = 10,000 random treatment assignments.” Printed calls (line breaks of the layout removed): p. 214, `possible_tr_assignment <- make_tr_vec_permutation(N, p, R = 10000, seed = 4224)`; p. 216 (PDF p. 8), `prob_exposure_sw <- make_exposure_prob(possible_tr_assignment, adj_matrix_sw, make_exposure_map_AS, list(hop = 1))`; p. 217 (PDF p. 9), `observed_tr_assignment <- make_tr_vec_permutation(N, p, R = 1, seed = 4224)`; p. 218 (PDF p. 10), `estimates_sw <- estimates(received_exposure_sw, observed_outcome_sw, prob_exposure_sw, control_condition = 'no')`, and the same calls for the second network.
(S7) Audit notation, not printed in the chapter. $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z},\theta_i)$ is the exposure unit $i$ receives and $Y_i = y_i(D_i)$ its observed outcome; the exposure mapping is taken as correctly specified, $y_i(\mathbf{z}) = y_i(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i))$ for every profile. $\pi_i(d) = \Pr(D_i = d) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d)$ and $\pi_{ij}(d,e) = \Pr(D_i = d, D_j = e)$, so $\pi_{ii}(d,d) = \pi_i(d)$ and $\pi_{ii}(d,e) = 0$ for $d \ne e$. $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{Var}$ and $\mathrm{Cov}$ are over the randomization distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ (and, where a target says so, over a simulated table of assignments); the population, the network, the mapping and the potential outcomes are fixed. The four-condition mapping is read with the treated-peer count $\theta_i\mathbf{z} = \sum_j\theta_{ij}z_j$ (P044-T9). The estimators are those computed by the staged R package interference (commit c3fc7b3; R/estimates.R and R/make_exposure_prob.R), whose documentation attributes them to Equations 1, 3, 7, 10, 11 and 15 of Aronow and Samii (2017). For marginal inputs $w_i(d) > 0$ and joint inputs $w_{ij}(d,e) \ge 0$ with $w_{ii}(d,d) = w_i(d)$, and with $I_i(d) = \mathbf{I}(D_i = d)$: [point estimator] $\widehat\mu(d) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i I_i(d)Y_i/w_i(d)$ and $\widehat\tau(k,l) = \widehat\mu(k) - \widehat\mu(l)$; [variance functional] $$\widehat V_d = \sum_{(i,j):\,w_{ij}(d,d)>0} I_i(d)I_j(d)\,Y_iY_j\left(\frac{1}{w_i(d)w_j(d)} - \frac{1}{w_{ij}(d,d)}\right) + \sum_{i\ne j:\,w_{ij}(d,d)=0}\left(\frac{I_i(d)Y_i^2}{2w_i(d)} + \frac{I_j(d)Y_j^2}{2w_j(d)}\right),$$ $$\widehat C_{kl} = \sum_{(i,j):\,w_{ij}(k,l)>0} I_i(k)I_j(l)\,Y_iY_j\left(\frac{1}{w_i(k)w_j(l)} - \frac{1}{w_{ij}(k,l)}\right) - \sum_{(i,j):\,w_{ij}(k,l)=0}\left(\frac{I_i(k)Y_i^2}{2w_i(k)} + \frac{I_j(l)Y_j^2}{2w_j(l)}\right),$$ $$\widehat V(k,l) = \frac{\widehat V_k + \widehat V_l - 2\widehat C_{kl}}{N^2},$$ all sums over ordered pairs, the first sum of $\widehat V_d$ and both sums of $\widehat C_{kl}$ including $i = j$. The exact inputs are $w = \pi$. The inputs the package returns from a table of $R$ assignments with counts $c_i(d)$ and $c_{ij}(d,e)$ are $w_i(d) = (c_i(d)+1)/(R+1)$, $w_{ij}(d,d) = c_{ij}(d,d)/(R+1)$ for $i \ne j$, and $w_{ij}(k,l) = c_{ij}(k,l)/R$ for $k \ne l$ and all $i, j$.
Scope of the list. No headline claim is a numbered result. P044-H2 (unbiasedness of the Horvitz–Thompson estimators) and P044-H4 (conservative variance estimators) are mathematical statements, and each is touched by a finding, so they enter as result_touched_by_finding targets (P044-T12, P044-T11) and there is no headline_result target. The clause of P044-H2 that Hajek or weighted least squares estimators are “consistent and considerably more efficient” is printed without hypotheses and defers to Aronow and Samii (2017), and the finding about it (P044-A002) was not confirmed; it is transcribed in P044-T12 and is not a target of its own (the formal statements belong to that paper, P013). P044-H1, H3, H9 and H10 describe the method and the package, and P044-H5 to H8 are simulation results and descriptions of the simulated networks. Six confirmed errors have corrections that change a mathematical statement and are targets: P044-N005 (Major; conservativeness of the variance estimators when the exposure probabilities are simulated), P044-E001 (Moderate; the support condition missing from the unbiasedness statement), P044-E002 (Moderate; the stated distribution of the simulated baseline outcomes), P044-E005 (Minor; the returned exposure probabilities are smoothed counts, so the implemented estimator is not exactly unbiased even with every assignment enumerated), P044-E007 (Minor; misprinted symbols in the no-interference statements and in the exposure-mapping display) and P044-E003 (Minor; the constant 0.7 for the within-community share of edges). P044-E002 and P044-E003 are descriptions of simulated inputs that disagree with the generators the printed code calls; they are listed because the correction replaces a stated distribution or constant, and each target says which premise is read from source code and lies outside what Lean can establish. The other confirmed errors are not targets because their corrections change no mathematical statement of the chapter: P044-E006, P044-E008 and P044-N014 (Moderate) are defects of the package code whose repair is a change of code (a missing value where a total is zero, a hard-coded control label, rejection of repeated draws in the Bernoulli samplers), and the validators find no statement of the chapter false on their account; P044-N009 (Moderate) is the scale label of the upper panel of Figure 16.3, established by re-running the simulation; P044-N004 and P044-N010 concern reproducibility; P044-N003 is a slip in reading Figure 16.1; P044-N012 is bibliographic. Findings classed as clarity notes, not confirmed or out of scope are outside the brief.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: ‘the variance estimators of these effects, which are conservative approximations to the exact variances’ (p. 217), with the statement on p. 213 that the methods of Aronow and Samii (2017) account conservatively for variance components
canonical_claim.location: p. 217 (PDF p. 9); p. 213 (PDF p. 5); Conclusion, pp. 219 and 221 (PDF pp. 11 and 13)
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 217 (PDF p. 9)] “Next, we estimate exposure-specific effects using both the Horvitz–Thompson and Hajek estimators, as well as the variance estimators of these effects, which are conservative approximations to the exact variances. Particularly, we estimate exposure effects as a contrast to the no exposure condition (or the control condition).”
[p. 213 (PDF p. 5)] “When it comes to statistical inference, the issues in this setting are the potentially complex dependencies across units, both in terms of outcomes but also, crucially, in the exposures that they receive. In the network in Figure 16.1, we can see that units 1 and 2 are both connected to unit 3, creating a dependency on whether these two units will receive indirect exposure. However, unit 2 is also tied to other peers of unit 3: units 5, 4, and 1. Such dependencies in exposure are a form of “multi-way clustering” that must be accounted for in statistical inference. Aronow and Samii (2017) propose sample theoretic methods for doing this in a way that conservatively accounts for variance components that cannot be directly estimated from the data.”
[Conclusion, pp. 219 and 221 (PDF pp. 11 and 13)] “Reliable inference in such settings requires that one address (a) potential confounding based on nonrandom variation in units’ network locations and (b) complex dependencies in the ways that a set of units might be subject to spillover effects through shared peers. We described an approach that addresses these complications through inverse probability weighted estimators.”
[What the estimators are computed from, as printed; line breaks of the layout removed] p. 214 (PDF p. 6): `possible_tr_assignment <- make_tr_vec_permutation(N, p, R = 10000, seed = 4224)`. p. 216 (PDF p. 8): `prob_exposure_sw <- make_exposure_prob(possible_tr_assignment, adj_matrix_sw, make_exposure_map_AS, list(hop = 1))`. p. 217: “We also need to assign treatment and compute units’ received exposure condition according to our assumed exposure scenario.” `observed_tr_assignment <- make_tr_vec_permutation(N, p, R = 1, seed = 4224)`. p. 218 (PDF p. 10): `estimates_sw <- estimates(received_exposure_sw, observed_outcome_sw, prob_exposure_sw, control_condition = 'no')`, with the outputs `estimates_sw$var_tau_ht` and `estimates_sw$var_tau_h`.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The chapter defines neither ‘conservative’ nor the variance estimators; Note 2 (p. 221): ‘For a formal discussion of the estimators, see Aronow and Samii (2017).’ The estimators are those of the staged package (standing assumptions S7); the exposure probabilities they use are the values computed from the 10,000 simulated assignments (S6). The effects are the contrasts $\tau(d,d_{00})$ of S5 for $d = d_{11}, d_{10}, d_{01}$. The sentence of p. 213 about units 5, 4 and 1 is the subject of P044-N003 (a slip in reading Figure 16.1) and is quoted only as context.
canonical_claim.note:
Listed because P044-N005 (Major) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. It is not a theorem of the chapter: no estimator is displayed and no hypothesis is stated. Its formalizable content, on the validators' reading, is the inequality $\mathrm E[\widehat V(k,l)] \ge \mathrm{Var}(\widehat\tau(k,l))$ for the variance functional of S7 at the inputs the recipe computes. For the Horvitz–Thompson estimator that inequality is refuted by P044-T1 when the inputs are simulated and proved in P044-T2 when they are the exact design probabilities and the contrasted exposures are supported; the expected result for this target is therefore ‘false as stated for simulated inputs, true under the hypotheses of P044-T2’, with no separate proof. For the Hajek variance estimator the chapter's wording asserts no finite-sample bound that could be stated (P044-N006, not confirmed). The reuse of seed 4224 on pp. 214 and 217 makes the realized assignment the first of the 10,000 simulated ones; the chapter does not mention it. The brief's priority scale has no level for a printed statement touched by a Major finding; 3 is used, as for an exact finite-sample statement, so that it follows the counterexample and the corrected statement.

Accepted review: distinguish the exact-probability, support-qualified HT variance theorem from finite simulation error. The qualified baseline small-world evidence is retained for the network regenerated from the printed code; its simulated-probability moments condition on the recorded assignment bank, and numerical/Monte Carlo qualifications and distinct table provenance remain material. It neither identifies the historical network nor shows a published table cell wrong. The two forty-unit R=10000 counterexample banks are different conditional tables, not replacements for one another or an average over all banks. Finite assignment simulation is a computational approximation, as finite bootstrap resampling is. Increasing the number of draws with suitable accuracy checks or proved simulation-error control is a possible remedy whose effort depends on the relevant joint exposure probabilities, smoothing and support handling. No universal R=10000 failure, draw threshold, invalidity of Monte Carlo, finite-R coverage guarantee or proof of the newly discussed bootstrap/hypergeometric/IID-limit formulas is claimed by these existing Lean records. The exact-input theorem, finite counterexamples, and Major classification are unchanged.

first_pass.notes: Claim-stage verdict unchanged. The original row and public description accurately disclose the selected universal reading and independent branch, but disclosure cannot identify that stronger proposition with the paper claim. The record’s “registered interpretation” is precisely the disputed attribution, not a newly discovered fact that corrects my reading. The published chapter pp. 214 and 217 uses the same seed for the assignment bank and observation and describes conservative approximations; it supplies no universal two-regime finite-R conjunction (https://cyrussamii.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BK-EEP-Chp16.pdf). Metadata: target_kind=result_touched_by_finding and status=counterexample_proved are consistent with an intended refutation, but resolution_kind=full_refutation_proved overstates coverage of the quoted printed target.

The exported negation can be established by failure of the independent branch alone and entails no failure of the seed-reused branch used in the printed workflow; negating this stronger conjunction is not the negation of the printed assertion.

evidence.second_review: P044/Wave1/SimulatedVariance.lean:32 negates PrintedSimulatedConservativeness, defined at P044/P044_NetworkSpillovers.lean:1216 as exact expected-variance dominance for every admissible finite bank in both independent and first-bank observation regimes, conjoined at P044/P044_NetworkSpillovers.lean:1234. coverage_judgments.notes: The sole credited row refutes an exact universal conjunction over independent observation and first-bank observation, with a failure of the former sufficient. The printed recipe reuses its seed; negating an added independent branch does not negate that recipe’s asserted behavior. The statement is mathematically meaningful and its domain is nonempty, but full_refutation_proved is inconsistent with attribution to the quoted target. No target split is registered. Source inspected: published chapter pp. 213–218, https://cyrussamii.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BK-EEP-Chp16.pdf; no external conditional theorem is involved.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Design-based inference, last sentences (p. 212): unbiased Horvitz-Thompson estimators of the $\tau(d,d')$ effects; with the explanation on p. 216
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 212 (PDF p. 4)] “Our goal is to obtain unbiased or consistent estimates of $\tau(d,d')$ effects and to be able to obtain informative and well-performing confidence intervals for statistical inference. With respect to bias, the issue in this setting is the nonrandom assignment of exposures despite random treatment assignment. Individual exposure is a function of both random treatment assignment and an individual’s network position, captured by their adjacency matrix row, $\theta_i$. Network position is nonrandom, and so this means that exposures are endogenous to potential confounding factors. For example, someone who has many direct peers has a much higher probability of receiving indirect exposure than someone with only a few peers. A unit’s number of peers could be related to nontreatment factors that affect outcomes, introducing confounding. Based on classical results from sampling theory, Aronow and Samii (2017) showed that such confounding can be removed with inverse probability weighting—specifically, by weighting the outcome data contributed by a given unit by the inverse of the probability of the exposure received by that unit. Moreover, with the network adjacency matrix and exposure mapping in hand, these probabilities of exposure can be computed directly from the experimental design. Specifically, one can simulate treatment assignments based on the experimental design, feed them through the exposure mapping for each unit, and then determine each unit’s probabilities of falling into any of the exposure conditions. The probabilities can be used to construct unbiased Horvitz-Thompson estimators of the $\tau(d,d')$ effects or consistent and considerably more efficient Hajek or weighted least squares estimators.”
[p. 216 (PDF p. 8)] “These exposure probabilities are generalized propensity scores that can then be used in Horvitz–Thompson estimators or other inverse probability weighted estimators, such as the Hajek estimator of exposure-specific causal effects.$^{2}$ Compared to the Hajek estimator, the Horvitz–Thompson often suffers from excessive variance, and although the bias of the Hajek estimator is not 0, it is typically small and worth the variance reduction. We now estimate exposure-specific effects. These are defined as contrasts between averages of individual potential outcomes across different exposures. To estimate the average potential outcome in a specific exposure condition, we have to take into account that we only observe the potential outcome for units in that specific exposure condition, and that the probability of observing potential outcomes in that specific exposure condition are not equal across units. This is precisely what inverse probability estimators like the Horvitz–Thompson take into account and the reason why we can obtain unbiased estimates of average potential outcomes in a specific exposure condition, and unbiased estimates of contrasts between these averages across different exposures.”
[Notes, p. 221 (PDF p. 13)] “1. Our networks do not have isolates, but we suggest researchers remove isolates from their analysis. 2. For a formal discussion of the estimators, see Aronow and Samii (2017).”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\tau(d,d')$ and the phrase ‘where $d$ and $d'$ are two different possible exposures’ (p. 212; standing assumptions S5); the designs the chapter admits, among them complete random assignment (pp. 210–211; S2); the exposure mapping (S4). The chapter displays no estimator; the Horvitz–Thompson estimator is $\widehat\mu_{HT}(d) - \widehat\mu_{HT}(d')$ with $\widehat\mu_{HT}(d) = \frac1N\sum_i\mathbf I(D_i = d)Y_i/\pi_i(d)$ (S7; staged package, documented as Equations 1 and 3 of Aronow and Samii (2017)). ‘The probabilities’ are the exposure probabilities $\pi_i(d)$ of each unit, which the passage says are obtained by simulating assignments.
canonical_claim.note: Listed because P044-E001 (Moderate) touches it; it is also the mathematical part of headline claim P044-H2. Formalizable content: for every design, network and exposure mapping of the setting and all real potential outcomes, $\mathrm E[\widehat\mu_{HT}(d) - \widehat\mu_{HT}(d')] = \tau(d,d')$. As printed, with no support condition, this is refuted by P044-T3 (a unit with $\pi_i(d) = 0$ makes the estimator undefined or, with the unobservable terms dropped, biased, and no other estimator is unbiased either); with $\pi_i(d) > 0$ and $\pi_i(d') > 0$ for every unit it is P044-T4(a). The expected result for this target is therefore ‘false as stated, true under the hypothesis of P044-T4’. Two further findings bear on the same sentences and have their own targets: the probabilities the recipe actually returns are smoothed counts (P044-E005; P044-T7, P044-T8). The clause ‘consistent and considerably more efficient Hajek or weighted least squares estimators’ is an asymptotic and comparative claim printed without hypotheses, for which the chapter refers to Aronow and Samii (2017); the finding about it (P044-A002) was not confirmed, and it is not a target here. The sentence on p. 216 that the bias of the Hajek estimator ‘is typically small’ is a qualitative remark and is not a target.

first_pass.notes: The printed prose does not explicitly state support, as confirmed by reading the published chapter pp. 212 and 216, but it also does not define a zero-support HT extension; S7 expressly specifies positive inputs. Thus this is a correct refutation of the registered stronger proposition, not an exact refutation on the estimator domain supplied in the packet. The record’s chosen global reading and zero-division disclosure do not resolve that fidelity mismatch; no claim-stage verdict is changed. Confidence is medium because the unqualified prose admits an alternative literal reading. Metadata scope note: the target also quotes asymptotic Hajek/WLS remarks, while its name and the row identify only the HT-unbiasedness component.

differences.what: PrintedUnbiasedness quantifies over every true-marginal weight array with each label possible at only some unit; S7 specifies the inverse-probability estimator for positive marginal inputs. The formal proposition therefore also asserts unbiasedness for weights outside the supplied estimator domain.

htTerm totalizes the zero-weight case, dropping unsupported contributions; neither the printed text nor the target definition of HT explicitly identifies its estimator with this zero-support extension. Negating that stronger universal assertion does not negate the positive-input assertion.

evidence.adjudicator: P044/Wave1/Unbiasedness.lean:14 negates PrintedUnbiasedness, whose definition at P044/P044_NetworkSpillovers.lean:1189 requires each label to be possible at some unit but permits zero true marginal probabilities at other units. In contrast, standing assumption S7 supplies the HT formula for positive marginal inputs and identifies exact inputs with the true probabilities; the four-unit-star witness has zero no-exposure probability at its center. The total htTerm definition at P044/P044_NetworkSpillovers.lean:93 extends the estimator beyond that supplied positive-input domain, so refuting unbiasedness of this extension does not refute the T12 estimator claim on its stipulated domain.
